Tumult
tū´mult
n. (uproar, disorderly commotion; rendering Hebrew hamon, Greek thorubos)
From Latin tumultus, an uproar. A tumult is noise with a crowd in it — agitation that has stopped being individual.

Biblical Definition

A tumult is a crowd's uproar. The chief priests plan Christ's arrest around it — “not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people” (Mat 26:5) — and Pilate yields when he “saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made” (Mat 27:24). The psalmist locates its source and its Master: God “stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people” (Psa 65:7), setting crowd-noise and ocean-noise in the same sentence as things only He quiets.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines tumult as the commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar and confusion of voices.

expand to see more

TUMULT, n. The commotion, disturbance or agitation of a multitude, usually accompanied with great noise, uproar and confusion of voices.

2. Violent commotion or agitation with confusion of sounds.

3. Agitation; high excitement; irregular or confused motion.

Key Scripture

Mat 26:5 — "But they said, Not on the feast day, lest there be an uproar among the people."

Mat 27:24 — "When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it."

Psa 65:7 — "Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people."

Act 21:34 — "And some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude: and when he could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle."

Modern Corruption

The crowd's roar is now manufactured on demand and mistaken for the voice of the people — and leaders, like Pilate, govern by measuring it.

expand to see more

Matthew 27:24 is the definitive account of leadership by tumult. Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, and he washed his hands and delivered an innocent man to be crucified. He had assessed the case correctly, said so publicly, and then made his decision on the basis of volume. Every leader who governs by the loudest available noise is standing in that basin, and the water has never yet cleaned anyone's hands.

Acts 21:34 supplies the comic detail that exposes what a tumult actually is: some cried one thing, some another, among the multitude; and when the chief captain could not know the certainty for the tumult, he commanded him to be carried into the castle. The crowd that nearly killed Paul could not have stated its own charge. Psalm 65:7 is the answer — the God who stills the sea's noise stills the people's, and He is not impressed by decibels.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hamon (H1995), a multitude, roar; Greek thorubos (G2351), an uproar, tumult — used of both mourning crowds and riots.

expand to see more

Hebrew hamon (H1995) — multitude, noise, tumult; Psalm 65:7, Isaiah 17:12, the rushing of nations.

Greek thorubos (G2351) — uproar, tumult; Matthew 26:5, 27:24, Acts 21:34.

Greek stasis (G4714) — insurrection, dissension; Acts 19:40, in danger to be called in question for this day's uproar.

Usage

"“Lest there be an uproar among the people” — the arrest timed around the crowd."

"“Rather a tumult was made” — Pilate governs by volume."

"“He stilleth… the tumult of the people” — the sea and the mob quieted by one hand."
